Pre-deal BRC: **A/B, Stable Incumbent shading to Quality Compounder.** FY2026 ROE

| Question | Base rate | Source |

| TAM-narrative capture rate (BRC now cites a $14B TAM) | Companies citing large TAMs typically capture well under a third of the projected share path | [Assumption] |

1.5-2. DEVIATION FROM BASE RATE AND MY JUSTIFICATION
My pre-haircut scenario weights implied a ~70% probability of an "at least fair"
IPS outcome — approximately 2x the ~35% M&A base rate. Per Step 1.5-3 this is a
RED FLAG requiring re-evaluation. Three company-specific justifications for a
deviation ABOVE base rate:
  (1) Brady's own capital-allocation record is demonstrably above average: ROE
      15.1%, 12 consecutive years of positive FCF, a -0.7% 3-yr net share count
      CAGR, and FY2026 buybacks executed at an average of $81.65 — BELOW today's
      price. [Actual, FY2026 filing/call]
  (2) The deal is funded at a management-stated cost BELOW 6% against a target
      that Honeywell ran at ~$1.1B revenue and that Brady guides to low-double-
      digit segment margin — an immediate positive spread over the cost of debt.
  (3) Management describes IPS as capex-light with a world-class Suzhou facility
      requiring no significant near-term investment — so the deal does not require
      a second capital commitment to work.

  (1) Honeywell — a sophisticated operator with full information — chose to divest

  (2) IPS economics are ~half of IDS at segment level. This is margin dilution, not
      margin accretion, and Dilution is the base case until proven otherwise.
  (3) Named live cost headwinds (memory tightness, electronics, diesel, Middle East
      logistics) fall on IPS's input stack specifically.

company-specific and documented). I HAVE reduced the bull probability and reduced
the bull-case value. Final weights: **Bear 35% / Base 45% / Bull 20%** (down from

plainly so the reader can see precisely how much of the conclusion is base-rate
discipline rather than company-specific judgment.

Brady manufactures specialty materials, printing systems and software that identify
and protect people, products and premises — labels, wire markers, lockout/tagout
devices, and the consumables that feed them (segment: IDS). As of 2026-08-03 it also
sells barcode scanners, mobile computing hardware and workflow-automation software
for logistics, retail, transportation and healthcare (segment: IPS, acquired from
Honeywell). Roughly 60% of pro-forma revenue is a high-margin consumables-and-
materials annuity; roughly 40% is a lower-margin hardware-and-software AIDC business
in which Brady claims the #2 market position.
Understandability: **HIGH** for IDS, **MEDIUM-LOW** for IPS (no segment history).

gets net leverage to roughly 2.0x, **tightly, with essentially no cushion for
integration costs or a demand air-pocket.** I therefore treat the "<2x in two

Post-deal, the combined engineering organisation implies further growth. This is a

Per the framework's explicit instruction, I use the FILED SBC series, not the

FY2026 operating leases $0.069B [Actual, SECTION 6B]. The company's own "net cash
$172.2M" definition excludes them. Capitalising them turns $172M of reported net
cash into ~$55M of net debt, and moves pro-forma adjusted net debt from ~$1.30B to
**~$1.33B.** I use $1.33B throughout. This is the more conservative and, I judge,
correct treatment.

No reliable Interbrand-style brand value is available for a specialty-materials
industrial of this size, and no DAU-type metric exists for IPS. **NOT ESTABLISHED
[Unconfirmed]. No intangible asset added.** I do not manufacture a number to
support a higher value.

GAAP ROIC proxy FY2026 = NOPAT (using the pack's broken/deferred tax inputs, so
using an imputed 22%) ÷ invested capital.
NOPAT = $0.263B × 0.78 = $0.205B. Invested capital = equity $1,358M + LT debt
$15M − cash $187M = $1,186M → GAAP ROIC ≈ **17.3%.**
R&D-capitalisation-adjusted ROIC ≈ **16.5–17.0%** — a gap of under 1pp, well inside
the framework's 5pp "explain it" threshold, so no further reconciliation is needed.
Cost of capital is ~8.4% (Section 3-4). **Pre-deal spread: ~+850bp. Genuinely a
good business.** Post-deal, blended ROIC falls because $1.0–1.1B of the $1.4B
purchase price sits in goodwill (non-earning), diluting the ratio arithmetically
regardless of operating performance. Post-deal blended ROIC on my FY2027 path:
NOPAT $226M ÷ invested capital (~$3.9B, including ~$1.0B of new goodwill) = **~5.8%**
in year one, rising toward ~9% by FY2031 as earnings build against a static goodwill
base. **This is the honest post-deal ROIC picture: the deal dilutes returns on
capital for several years even if everything goes right.** The framework's Engine-1
discipline does not permit hiding this inside a DCF.

Δ working capital (WC rose from $292M to $333M, i.e. a $41M USE of cash) ...

Cross-check via the cash-flow route: FCF $0.193B − SBC $0.023B = $0.170B →
**$3.56/share.**
The two routes differ by the working-capital treatment; the range is
**$2.95–$3.56/share**, call it ~$3.25/share owner earnings.
Against $87.43, that is **~27x owner earnings.** Compare with the reported multiple
of 21.6x FCF/share, 16.5x GAAP EPS ($4.29), and 16.5x adjusted EPS ($5.29).
The four multiples tell four different stories, and the differences are entirely
definitional. The number I trust most for valuation is the FCF-based one after SBC.

3.5-1 COMPETITIVE RESPONSE SIMULATION: SCORE -2
  Brady has entered, with $1.15B of scale, the exact market where Zebra
  Technologies is dominant and where Chinese vendors (Newland, Urovo) attack
  on price. Auto-ID hardware has 4-6 credible global vendors and a
  history of price deflation per unit. A rational Zebra response to Brady
  converting a Honeywell channel into a Brady channel is to defend the
  large logistics/retail accounts aggressively during the ownership
  transition — precisely the moment when the customer's incumbent supplier
  has changed hands. Management itself lists "customer retention" as a
  closing risk [Actual]. This is the highest-probability value-destruction
  channel and it is not visible in the guided year, because FY2027 guidance
  assumes the accounts stay.
  Counter-consideration (why not -3): Brady's IDS customer base is
  fragmented MRO/industrial with genuinely high switching costs, and those
  customers are not contested by Zebra at all. The competitive threat is
  contained to one segment.

3.5-2 REFLEXIVITY CHECK (Soros): SCORE -1, NET MILD NEGATIVE
  Positive channels: Brady's SBC is only $23M on a $4.1B cap, so the
  "high price → talent attraction" loop is immaterial. Funding is secured
  ($1B facility maturing 2031), so funding-difficulty reflexivity is absent.
  Negative channel, and it is real: Brady is a supplier telling large
  enterprise customers "we just borrowed 2.5x EBITDA to buy your platform."
  Procurement and supply-chain-risk functions at large logistics and retail
  customers explicitly score supplier leverage. That is a negative
  reflexive loop between balance sheet and revenue retention — and it feeds
  directly into the retention risk in 3.5-1. Net: -1.

3.5-3 CUSTOMER BEHAVIOR EVOLUTION
  IDS: mature, mainstream-to-late-adopter demand, driven by regulation.
  Penetration is not a variable — compliance is. LTV/CAC is stable and
  favourable. This is the good half of the company.
  IPS: this is where the life-cycle risk sits. Brady has bought a mature,
  mainstream auto-ID installed base at the point where the customer's
  relationship was with HONEYWELL. The transition from "Honeywell
  Productivity Solutions" to "Brady IPS" is exactly the moment at which
  large-account churn spikes, and the pack holds no churn, retention,
  LTV/CAC, or contract-duration data for it. [Unconfirmed]. I carry this
  uncertainty explicitly into the bear case rather than assuming retention.
